parole.significato: pious, devout (religious in a serious way)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vrome, from Proto-Germanic *frumô, related to German fromm, Dutch vroom (“pious”). In Old Saxon and Old High German, it is a noun meaning "use, benefit", but later it is used as an adjective.
From frugt (“fruit”) + -bar, from Middle Low German vruchtbar (“frugiferous”). Cognate with Dutch vruchtbaar and German fruchtbar.

From Middle Low German vruchten, from Proto-Germanic *furhtijaną, cognate with German fürchten.
From frygte (“to fear”) + -lig. After Middle Low German vruchtelik.

From Middle Low German vrouweken, vrouken, a diminutive of vrouwe, vruwe, from Old Saxon frūa. From Middle Low German vūchten (“to moisten”). Compare German feuchten.

From Middle Low German vundich. Related to fyndig.

parole.significato: quitting time (the time after the end of a workday)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vīrāvent and German Feierabend, a compound of Feier (“celebration”) + Abend (“evening”). Compare Norwegian Bokmål fyrabend, Swedish fyraben.
From Middle Low German firen (“celebrate”, literally “keep free”), from Latin fērior (“to rest from work, celebrate”), but probably influenced by fur (“hard situation, e.g. from criticism”).

parole.significato: to light, fire up (to keep a fire going)

parole.significato: to fence (with swords, as a sport)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vechten.
From Middle Low German velge, from Proto-Germanic *felgō.

parole.significato: prison (place of long-term confinement for those convicted of serious crimes)
parole.testo: Equivalent to fange (“to capture”) + -sel (“act of”). From Old Danish fengelse (“prison”), borrowed from Middle Low German vangnisse, vengnisse, cf. German Gefängnis. Icelandic fangelsi and Swedish fängelse are also borrowed from Low German.
From Middle Low German vesteninge (“fortress”), from vesten (“to fasten, to secure”), from Old Saxon fast (“firm, secure”). Equivalent to fæstne (“fasten, secure”) + -ning and fæste + -ning.

parole.significato: a male cousin (son of one's parent's sibling)
parole.testo: From Old Danish fædder (“paternal uncle, male cousin”), from Middle Low German vedder (“paternal uncle, male cousin, fraternal nephew”). Compare German Vetter, Old English fædera, Latin patruus, Ancient Greek πάτρως (pátrōs).
From Middle Low German vȫgen, from Proto-Germanic *fōgijaną, cognate with English fay, German fügen.
From Middle Low German vȫge (“adjustment”), derived from the verb. Compare German Fug.

From Middle Low German gans or Middle Dutch gansch; both from Old High German ganz (“whole, entire, sound, complete”), from Proto-West Germanic *gant (“all, whole, complete”).

parole.significato: to tan (to treat animal skins with tanning agents to turn them into leather)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German garwen, gerwen. Compare German gerben, Dutch gerven.

parole.significato: ear; the faculty of pitch (the ability to distinguish tones from each other)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German gehor; compare with German Gehör. From the same root as høre (“hear”).
From Middle Low German gemene (“common”), from Proto-Germanic *gamainiz. Cognate with English mean and German gemein.
From Old Danish girigh. Borrowed from Middle Low German girich. Cognates include also Swedish girig, Norwegian Bokmål gjerrig and German gierig

From Middle Low German gicht, a cognate of German Gicht, from Proto-Germanic *jihtiz.
From Middle Low German and German glatt. Related to glad.
From Middle Low German gliden.

parole.significato: ferocious, wild (likely to attack or bite)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German glupesch. Equivalent to glube + -sk, similarly to bidsk. Compare Norwegian and Swedish glupsk.
Perhaps Derived from Middle Low German klut (“lump”).

parole.significato: count (a nobleman, of the highest rank in Denmark, since 1849 without privileges; equivalent to a British earl)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German grēve, from Old Saxon grāvio, from Proto-West Germanic *grāfijō.

parole.significato: county, the domain of a count (nobleman)
parole.testo: From Old Danish grevæskap, from Middle Low German greveschap. Equivalent to greve + -skab.
From Middle Low German grof.
From Middle Low German grus, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *greutą (“grit”).

parole.significato: border (the line or frontier area separating regions)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German grenitze, grense, compare German Grenze, borrowed from Old Polish granica, from Proto-Slavic *granica.

parole.significato: Greek (of or relating to Greece, the Greek people, or the Greek language)
parole.testo: From Old Danish gretzsk, borrowed from Middle Low German grekesch, = greke + -sch (“a Greek”). Cf. also Swedish grekisk and German griechisch. The noun is derived from the adjective.

Older græskarve n pl, a compound of græs (“grass”) and Middle Low German korvet, korves, Old High German kurbiz (cf. German Kürbis, Swedish kurbits). It is an old loan from Latin cucurbita. Ultimately it derives from Sanskrit चिर्भट (cirbhaṭa), चर्भट (carbhaṭa, “cucumber”).

parole.significato: a badger (in particular the European badger, Meles meles)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German grevink (and grevel), derived from the verb graven (“to dig”), from Proto-Germanic *grabaną (Danish grave). The word has replaced older taks, from Proto-Germanic *þahsuz.
From Middle Low German gunst, from Old Saxon unst, from Proto-West Germanic *unsti, from Proto-Germanic *undiz.
From Middle Low German gunstich. Equivalent to gunst + -ig.
From an old expression 'gøre gæk af' or 'gøre for gæk' (“to mock, riducule”). The word is from Middle Low German geck. Compare German Geck.
From Middle Low German gȫkelen, cognate with German gaukeln (Swedish gyckla also comes from Low German). Probably, at least partially, borrowed from Latin joculor (“to joke”).
Equivalent to gøgle (“to juggle”) + -er (agent noun), from Middle Low German gȫkeler, cognate with German Gaukler.

parole.significato: armour covering the torso of a medieval knight
parole.testo: Via Middle Low German harnasch, harnisch, from Old French hernois.
From Middle Low German hast, from Old French haste. Cognate with Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌹𐍆𐍃𐍄 (haifst).
From Middle Low German hastich.

parole.significato: hero (a person who shows great courage and carries out extraordinary deeds)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German helt (“hero”) or German Held (“hero”), from Proto-Germanic *haliþaz (“hero”).

parole.significato: Used with a verb, indicating a movement towards or to something.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German hen, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *hiz (“here”). Related to Swedish hän, English hence, and German hin.
Borrowed from Middle Low German herkomst, German Herkunft. A verbal noun of German herkommen.
From Middle Low German herlik, derived from Old High German her. Compare Old English har.

From Middle Low German hertoch. Cognate to German Herzog, Dutch hertog.
Derived from hertug with the female affix + -inde. Hertug is from Middle Low German. Cognate to German Herzog, Dutch hertog.

parole.significato: to crave, yearn, aspire to, long for
parole.testo: Likely (onomatopoeia). Perhaps from Middle Low German hichen higen. Compare Norwegian hike.

From Middle Low German hengest, hengst, hingest, hingst, from Proto-Germanic *hangistaz, cognate with German Hengst. The Scandinavian word for “horse”, e.g. Danish hest, comes from a Verner alternation variant, *hanhistaz.

parole.significato: crowd, multitude (a large amount of people or animals)
parole.testo: From Old Danish hob, from Middle Low German hōp, from Old Saxon hōp, from Proto-West Germanic *haup (“heap”), cognate with English heap. Late Old Norse hópr and Swedish hop are also borrowed from Low German.
From Middle Low German hōpen, derived from the noun hōp (Danish hob). The verb has also been borrowed to Norwegian hope, Swedish hopa.

parole.significato: lots of, loads of (normally with the indefinite article and a following appositional noun)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German hōpen, the oblique form of hōp(e), see hob. Compare German ein Haufen (“loads of”).

parole.significato: court (family and society of a sovereign)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German hof, from Old Saxon hof, from Proto-West Germanic *hof, from Proto-Germanic *hufą, cognate with German Hof (“yard, court, farmyard”), Dutch hof (“yard, court, garden”), Old Norse hof (“shrine; court”). Doublet of hov (“shrine, temple”).
From Middle Low German hufte.
From Middle Low German hōmōt, a compound of hō (“high”) + mōt (“courage, mood”). Compare Swedish högmod, German Hochmut, Dutch hoogmoed.
From Middle Low German huseren. Compare German hausieren.
From Middle Low German hūsgerād. Compare German Hausgerät.

From Middle Low German hǖlen, from Old Saxon *hūwilon, from Proto-West Germanic *hūilōn.
From Middle Low German hǖpich, cognate with German häufig. Derived from the verb hūpe / Haufen (“heap”), from Proto-Germanic *hūpō. Related to *haupaz (English heap and, via Low German, Danish hob).

parole.significato: to employ, hire, appoint (often for specific tasks)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German hüren.
From Middle Low German hüre.

parole.significato: livewell, corf (a wooden box for storing living fish in a boat)
parole.testo: Equivalent to hytte (“to protect”) + fad (“barrel”), a calque of Middle Low German hǖdevat, German Hütefass.
From Middle Low German hōpen (“to hope”), from Old Saxon hopōn, from Proto-West Germanic *hopōn.
From Middle Low German hōn (“derision”).

parole.significato: to enforce, maintain, uphold (law, principle etc.)

From Middle Low German hanteren, influenced by hånd.

From hån + -e, from Middle Low German hônen, from Old Saxon hōnian, from Proto-West Germanic *haunijan. Compare Swedish håna.

parole.significato: to fence (to sell stolen goods as a middleman)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German hēlen, from Proto-Germanic *helaną (“to hide, conceal”), cognate with German hehlen (“to fence”) and Dutch helen (“to fence”).

parole.significato: to hamper, impede, inhibit, stunt, hinder

From Middle Low German klōk.

parole.significato: scholarly knowledge, knowledge gained through study
parole.testo: From Middle Low German kuntschap. By surface analysis, kund (“known”, obsolete) + -skab; compare kundgøre.

From Middle Low German kunstich. Equivalent to kunst + -ig.
From Middle Low German kunstener, derived from kunst. Cf. also Swedish konstnär and German Künstler.
Inherited from Old Danish korw, borrowed from Middle Low German korf, from Old Saxon *korf, from Proto-West Germanic *korb.
From Middle Low German qualm. Cognate with German Qualm, German quellen and Dutch kwalm.

From Middle Low German quede (“quince”), from Latin cydōnium (quidōnium), from Ancient Greek κυδώνιον μῆλον (kudṓnion mêlon), lit. "apples from the city of Kydonia" (modern Chania on Crete). Compare also German Quitte (hence Swedish kvitten). English quince comes via French coing from a different La

parole.significato: to injure, wound, maim (often in connection with an accident)
parole.testo: Formed from the past participle kvæst of an older verb kvæsse. Ultimately from Middle Low German quessen, quetsen. Compare Swedish kväsa.
From Middle Low German kundich.
From Middle Low German kūsch, from Proto-West Germanic *kūski, cognate with German keusch, Dutch kuis, Old English cūsċ. Borrowed from Latin cōnscius (“conscious”).
From Middle Low German kost, from Old French coste (“coast, side”), from Latin costa (“rib, side”).
Probably from Middle Low German keve, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kebutaz. Doublet of kæft.
From Middle Low German kede, cognate with German Kette. Borrowed from Latin catēna (“chain”).
From Middle Low German kempe, presumably related to Etymology 2 below in the sense of "champion," "warrior."
From Middle Low German kempen, from Old Saxon kempio, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *kamp (“battlefield”). Compare Swedish kämpa.
Via Middle Low German ketter, from Latin catharus, from Ancient Greek καθαροί (katharoí, “the pure”), referring to the Catharist sect.

From Middle Low German kōpman, from Old Saxon kōpman, from Proto-West Germanic *kaupamann, cognate with English chapman and German Kaufmann. Equivalent to købe (“buy”) + mand (“man”). Possibly partially inherited from Old Norse kaupmaðr, the native parallel to the Low German.
From Middle Low German kȫken(e) (also as kȫke), from Old Saxon *kukina, from Proto-West Germanic *kukinā, from Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna.

parole.significato: to hand, pass (in a careless manner)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German langen (“to reach for”), from Proto-Germanic *langōną, cognate with German langen, English long, Old Norse langa.
From Middle Low German lanksam, lanksum, from Proto-West Germanic *langasam (“lengthy, long-lasting”).
From Middle Low German las (“patch, scrap”).
From Middle Low German last, from the verb laden (“to transport”), from Old Saxon hladan.
From Middle Low German legelik. Trumped by belejlig.

From Middle Low German legelicheit (“situation”), form the adjective legelik (“situated”). Compare Middle Low German legenhēt (“situation, opportunity”) (whence Swedish lägenhet (“apartment”)) from legen (“lying”) and German Gelegenheit (“opportunity”) from gelegen (“lying”).
From Old Danish legsæ, lexe. Borrowed via Middle Low German lectie, lexe from Latin lēctiō (“reading”). Compare also Swedish läxa.
From Middle Low German limpen.
From Middle Low German limpe, derived from the verb.
By surface analysis, lempe + -lig. From Middle Low German limpelik. Compare Swedish lämplig.

parole.significato: fief (a land given by a sovereign to a vassal in exchange for military services, especially in the Middle Ages)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German lēn, from Old Saxon lēhan, from Proto-West Germanic *laihn, from Proto-Germanic *laihną (“loan”), cognate with German Lehn (Swedish län is a loan from Low German). Doublet of lån.
From Middle Low German levereren, leveren, from French livrer (“to deliver”), from Latin liberare (“to free”).

From Middle Low German lîden, from Old Saxon lithan; related to lide (“to proceed”), see below. The Low German word has also been borrowed into late Old Norse líða, Norwegian Bokmål lide, li, and Swedish lida.

parole.significato: tolerable, bearable (which one can tolerate or endure, is not too strict, or weighs too heavily)
parole.testo: lide (“to endure (archaic)”) + -lig, from Middle Low German lidelik.
From ligne + -else. After Middle Low German līkenisse, gelīkenisse, from Old Saxon gilīknessi, cognate with English likeness, German Gleichnis, Dutch gelijkenis.
From Middle Low German linnen, līnen.

parole.significato: lispound (unit of weight equal to about 8 kilograms)
parole.testo: Derived from Middle Low German livespunt.
Borrowed from Middle Low German lōt, from Old Saxon lōd, from Proto-West Germanic *laud, possibly borrowed from Gaulish *loudon, from Proto-Celtic *ɸloudom (“lead”).
From Middle Low German lōden.
From Middle Low German los, from Old Saxon lohs, from Proto-West Germanic *luhs.
From Middle Low German or Dutch lossen
From Middle Low German lōve, from Proto-Germanic *galaubô, cognate with German Glaube.

From Middle Low German luft, lucht (“air, smell”), from Old Saxon luft, from Proto-West Germanic *luftu. Probably influenced by German Luft (“air”). It is a cognate of Danish loft (“attic”) and Danish lugt (“smell”).

From Middle Low German lucht, luft (“air, smell”), from Old Saxon luft, from Proto-West Germanic *luftu, from Proto-Germanic *luftuz. Cognate with German Luft (“air”) and Old Norse loft (“attic, air”) (whence Danish loft (“attic”)). Danish luft (“air”) is borrowed from the older form of the Low Germ
From Middle Low German lūne (“lunar phase, caprice”), from Latin lūna. Cognate with German Laune.
Borrowed from Middle Low German lute (“lute”).
From Middle Low German lūtter (“clean, pure, unmixed”).

From Old Danish lyktæ, borrowed from Middle Low German lūchte, from Proto-Germanic *liuhtijô, cognate with German Leuchte. Derived from Proto-Germanic *leuhtą (“light”), cf. English light and German Licht.

parole.significato: to be a success, be successful, succeed in (with a noun phrase or a noun clause as its subject and the person succeedin…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German lucken (“to succeed”), a cognate of German glücken (“to succeed”). Norwegian Bokmål lykkes and Swedish lyckas are also borrowed from Low German. The verb is derived from the noun Middle Low German (ge)lucke (“happiness, good luck”) (Danish lykke, German Glück).
From Middle Low German lückesālich (“lucky, happy”). Compare Swedish lycksalig.
From Old Danish lyst, lust, from Middle Low German lust, from Old Saxon lust, from Proto-West Germanic *lustu. Cognate with English lust and German Lust. A different stem in Old Norse losti.
From Middle Low German lüstern (“hear, listen”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German lecker. Compare Norwegian lekker, Swedish läcker and Dutch lekker.

From Middle Low German lēren, from Proto-Germanic *laizijaną, cognate with German lehren (“teach”), Dutch leren, and Gothic 𐌻𐌰𐌹𐍃𐌾𐌰𐌽 (laisjan). Late Old Norse læra, Norwegian lære, and Swedish lära are also borrowed from Low German. For sense development from "teach" → "learn", compare Russian учи́ть

parole.significato: teachings, doctrine, theory (a coherent system of thoughts or ideas in science or religion)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German lēre, from Proto-Germanic *laizō (“teaching”), cognate with English lore, German Lehre, Dutch leer, and Gothic 𐌻𐌰𐌹𐍃𐍉 (laisō). Norwegian lære and Swedish lära are also borrowed from Low German.
From Middle Low German lofte, from the verb loven, from Old Saxon lovon (“to praise”).
From Middle Low German mak (“ease, calm”), related to Old Saxon makon (“to make”).

From Middle Low German māken, from Old Saxon makōn, from Proto-West Germanic *makōn, cognate with English make, German machen, Dutch maken. Old Norse maka, Norwegian make, Swedish maka are also borrowed from Low German. The verb is derived from the adjective Proto-Germanic *makaz (“suitable”). A rat
From Middle Low German macht, from Proto-Germanic *mahtiz, derived from the verb from *maganą (“to be able”). Cognate with English might and German Macht. The Old Norse form was máttr (from *mahtuz).

From Middle Low German mālen (“to draw, paint”), from Old Saxon mālōn, from Proto-West Germanic *mālōn, from Proto-Germanic *mēlōną, which could be related to *mailą (“spot, blemish, mark”). Cognate with Icelandic mála (“to paint”).
From Middle Low German manen (“to remind”), from Old Saxon manōn, from Proto-Germanic *manōną, cognate with German mahnen.

parole.significato: marsh (low wet-land, from time to time flooded by the tide, especially with reference to the North Sea)
parole.testo: From Old Danish mersk, borrowed from Middle Low German marsch, mersch, from Proto-West Germanic *marisk, cognate with English marsh (Norwegian marsk and German Marsch are also from Low German). A compound from *mari (“sea”) + *-isk (“-ish”).

parole.significato: marshal (a military officer ranking over a general)
parole.testo: Older marskalk, borrowed from Middle Low German marschalk, from Old Saxon *marhskalk, from Proto-West Germanic *marhaskalk, from *marh (“horse”) + *skalk (“servant”). Cognate with German Marschall, Old High German marahscalc and borrowed to Old French mareschal (hence English marshal). The modern Da
Borrowed from Middle Low German mast, from Old Saxon *mast, from Proto-West Germanic *mast.
From Middle Low German medegift.
medliden + -hed, from Middle Low German medelidheit, medeliden, a calque of Latin compassiō, from Ancient Greek σῠμπᾰ́θειᾰ (sŭmpắtheiă). Compare Swedish medlidande.
From Middle Low German melden.
Chiefly from Middle Low German men, man (“just, but”). To some extent merged with Old Norse meðan (“while”), whence medens, mens.

parole.significato: to mean (to have a certain meaning in mind)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German meinen, mēnen (“to mean”), from Proto-Germanic *mainijaną, cognate with English mean, Dutch menen, German meinen (Icelandic meina and Swedish mena are also borrowed from Low German).
From Old Danish men, from Middle Low German mene.
Via Middle Low German misse, Old Saxon missa from Medieval Latin missa, a past participle of the verb mittō (“to send”).
From Middle Low German middel, from Old Saxon middil, from Proto-Germanic *midlą. The noun is derived from the adjective.
From Middle Low German middelmātich. Compare Dutch middelmatig, German mittelmäßig and Swedish medelmåttig.
From Middle Low German mite.
From Middle Low German mink, menk, from Old Saxon mink, menk, of obscure ultimate origin.
From Middle Low German mishandelen.
mis- + tanke, from Middle Low German misdünken. Unrelated to English mistake.
From Middle Low German mos, from Proto-Germanic *mōsą (“mush, porridge”).
Equivalent to mund (“mouth”) + -lig (adjective). From Middle Low German muntlik.
From a diminutive form of Old Danish mussel, from Middle Low German mussele, muschele, from Latin musculus.

parole.significato: of age; having reached the age of majority
parole.testo: From Middle Low German mundich. Related to Old Norse mund. and Latin manus.
From Middle Low German muterie.
From Middle Low German matelik (“appropriate. moderate”). Equivalent to måde + -lig.
From Middle Low German maltit.
From må (“may, might”) + ske (“happen”), after Middle Low German machschēn (“mayhap”). Compare with Norwegian kanskje and Swedish kanske. Compare also English mayhap and Dutch misschien.
From Middle Low German matte from Medieval Latin matta, of Semitic origin. Cognate include English mat and German Matte.
From Middle Low German mekelen.
From Middle Low German munsteren (“scrutinize”).
From Middle Low German nachtegale, from Old Saxon nahtagala, from Proto-West Germanic *nahtigalā.
navn + -lig, from Middle Low German namelike. Related to nemlig.
From Middle Low German nēderdêl. Compare Middle High German niderteil (whence obsolete German Niederteil); compare also Swedish nederdel (literally “the bottom part”).
From Middle Low German nedderich (“low”), derived from Middle Low German nedder
From Middle Low German negelken (“little nail”), referring to its clove, from Old Saxon nagal.

parole.significato: that is, that is to say
parole.testo: From Middle Low German nemlik. Cognate to German nämlich.

parole.significato: nod (to incline the head up and down)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German nicken.
From Middle Low German nōch, from Old Saxon ginōg, cognate with Old Norse nógr, gnógr, English enough, German genug.
From nyde (“enjoy”) + -lig, from Middle Low German nūtlik. Compare German niedlich.

parole.significato: nettle (any plant from the genus Urtica)
parole.testo: From Old Danish nætlæ, borrowed from Middle Low German nettele, from Old Saxon netila.
From Middle Low German neren, from Old Saxon nerian, from Proto-West Germanic *naʀjan, from Proto-Germanic *nazjaną (“to rescue, heal”), causative of *nesaną (“to survive, recover”).

From Middle Low German nōttorft, from Old Saxon nōdthurft, from nōd (“need”) + thurft (“need”). Compare Gothic 𐌽𐌰𐌿𐌳𐌹𐌸𐌰𐌿𐍂𐍆𐍄𐍃 (naudiþaurfts), German Notdurft, Dutch nooddruft, and (from Low German) Swedish nödtorft.
From nødtørft (“necessity”) + -ig, after Middle Low German nōttroftich, German notdürftig, Dutch nooddruftig.
From Middle Low German nochaftik, compare with Norwegian Bokmål nøyaktig and Swedish nöjaktig.

From Middle Low German olt, old, from Proto-Germanic *aldaz. Cognate with English old, Dutch oud, and German alt. The adjective exists in the Scandinavian languages only in the comparative and superlative, cf. ældre, ældst.
From Old Danish aldæfathær and Middle Low German oldevader.
From Middle Low German oldemōder.
From Old Danish oliæ, borrowed via Middle Low German oli(e) from Latin oleum (“olive oil”). Compare Swedish olja, German Öl, Dutch olie. English oil has gone through French huile.
From Old Danish oliuæ, borrowed via Middle Low German olīve and Old French olive from Latin olīva (“olive”). Cf. also Swedish oliv, German Olive, Dutch olijf, English olive.
Formed after Middle Low German uphoren. Compare German aufhören.
From Middle Low German uprichtich.

parole.significato: rebellion, revolt, insurrection, rising, uprising (protest against a leadership)
parole.testo: Formally a verbal noun of oprøre (“to shock”). Borrowed from Middle Low German uprōr, cognate with German Aufruhr m and Dutch oproer (whence English uproar). The word replaced an older, related noun with a similar meaning: Proto-Germanic *hrōzō, cf. Old Saxon hrōra, Old High German hruora, German Ru
Equivalent to op (“up”) + sigt (“sight”), borrowed from Middle Low German upsicht, a verbal noun of upsēn (“to oversee”). Compare also German Aufsicht and aufsehen.
From Middle Low German orden, from Latin ōrdō (“order, rank”). Doublet of ordre.

parole.significato: to order, arrange, organize (to put in the right sequence)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German ordenen, from Latin ōrdināre (“to arrange, govern”). Compare Swedish ordna, German ordnen.
From Middle Low German orloch, orloge. Related to Old Norse ørlǫg
From Middle Low German ōst (“east”), from Proto-Germanic *austrą. Cognate of Danish øster, Danish øst.
From Middle Low German overdat. Compare Dutch overdaad.
From Middle Low German overdadich. Equivalent to overdåd + -ig. Cognate of Dutch overdadig.
Equivalent to over (“over”) + flod (“flood”), from Middle Low German overflōt, calque of Latin superfluitās. Compare German Überfluss.
Equivalent to overflod (“abundance”) + -ig, from Middle Low German overflōdich, calque of Latin superfluus. Compare German überflüssig.
From Middle Low German overlegen, a past participle of overliggen (“to oppress”), from over- (“over”) + liggen (“to lie”). Compare German überlegen (“superior”).
over- + mod. From Middle Low German overmod. Compare German Übermut, Swedish övermod.

From over (“over”) + sætte (“place, put, set”). From Middle Low German ȫversetten, ōversetten, from Old Saxon *ovarsettian, from Proto-West Germanic *ubarsattjan. Compare Swedish översätta and Norwegian Bokmål oversette.
Equivalent to over + veje. From Middle Low German overwegen. Compare Swedish överväga, Dutch overwegen, and, with a different prefix, German erwägen.

parole.significato: (is only found in a few compound words) package
parole.testo: From Middle Low German pack; same word as pakke (“parcel, package”), which see.
From Middle Low German pakken, from packe. See Etymology 1 above.

parole.significato: panel (most senses, e.g. a wall panel, a panel of experts)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German panele (“wall covering”), from Latin panullus, diminutive of pannus.

parole.significato: pawn (item sold to a pawn shop)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German pant.
From Middle Low German papegoie, papagoie, from Old French papagai, or from Spanish papagayo.
From Middle Low German papir, pappir, from Old French papier.
From late Old Danish par, from Middle Low German par, from Latin pār.
From Middle Low German passen, from French passer, with semantic development "let time pass" > "wait, expect", "take care of".
From Middle Low German pauwelon or paulun (“pavilion”), from French pavilion.
From Middle Low German pedell, bedell, from Medieval Latin pedellus, bedellus, bidellus.

From Middle Low German petersilie, from Medieval Latin petrocilium, from Latin petroselinum, from Ancient Greek πετροσέλινον (petrosélinon, “parsley”), from πέτρος (pétros, “rock, stone”) and σέλινον (sélinon, “celery”).
From Middle Low German pīpe, from Medieval Latin pipa (“pipe, flute”), derived from Latin pīpō (“to pip, peep”). Cognate with late Old Norse pípa, German Pfeife, English pipe, and French pipe.
From Middle Low German pīpen, from Latin pīpō (“to pip, peep”). Cognate with German pfeifen.
From Middle Low German pilere, pilar, from Medieval Latin pilare, pilarium, from Latin pīla (“pillar”).
From Middle Low German pille, from Medieval Latin pilla, pillula, from Latin pilula, diminutive of pila (“ball”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German pīnen, derived from the noun.
Equivalent to pine (“torment”) + lig. From Middle Low German pīnlik, cf. German peinlich, which has influenced the semantic development of the Danish word.
Probably from Middle Low German pissen from Old French pissier, from Vulgar Latin *pīssiāre.

parole.significato: to make a whining, high-pitched sound
parole.testo: From Middle Low German pipen, from Latin pipare. Doublet of pibe (“to pipe, play a pipe”).
Likely from Middle Low German palte.

Via Middle Low German plātze and Old French place from Latin platēa, a loan from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa), substantive of πλατύς (platús, “broad”). The Low German form was also borrowed to Late Old Norse plaz and Swedish plats.
From Middle Low German plante, from Latin planta. Doublet of klan.
Borrowed via Middle Low German platt from Old French plat, from Vulgar Latin *plattus, which probably is loan from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús), a cognate of Danish flad.
From Middle Low German plicht, from Proto-West Germanic *plihti (“care, duty”).

parole.significato: obligated, (someone who has a duty to do something (according to laws and regulations))
parole.testo: From Middle Low German plichtich, derived from Middle Low German plicht (“penalty, punishment, duty”).
From Middle Low German plutzlik, from the onomatopoeic/exclamatory plotz (“splash”).
From Middle Low German plunderen, plünderen (“to plunder”). Cognate with German plündern.
From Middle Low German pote (“small stick”).

parole.significato: to graft (attach a cut plant part to another plant, either under the bark or at the end of a branch, and cause the plan…
parole.testo: From Middle Low German poten (“to poke with a stick”)

parole.significato: a blemish or rash resulting from smallpox, pockmarks, also similar conditions from syphilis, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German pocke (“boil, abscess”), from Proto-Germanic *pukkaz, *pukkǭ (“pock; swelling”), cognate with English pock, pox, German Pocke. Maybe kopper (“smallpox”) is a euphemistic refashioning of this word.

Via Middle Low German politīe and Medieval Latin politia from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía, “citizenship, government”), derived from the noun πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”), from the noun πόλις (pólis, “city, state”).

parole.significato: pump, tap, faucet (an outdoor water pump)
parole.testo: Via Middle Low German post from Latin postis (“post, door-post”).
From Middle Low German pote, of uncertain ultimate origin; perhaps equivalent to the Romance cognates of French patte, from Vulgar Latin *pauta, a borrowing from a substrate language.

parole.significato: prick (the feeling of being pierced or punctured by an object with a fine point, the action of pricking)
parole.testo: Formed from the verb prikke (“to poke lightly”), from Middle Low German pricke (“a prick”), pricken (“to prick”), from Old Saxon *prikkian, from Proto-Germanic *prikjaną.

parole.significato: prince (son or male-line grandson of a reigning monarch)
parole.testo: Via Middle Low German prinze, German Prinz from Old French prince, from Latin prīnceps. Doublet of fyrste via a calque.
From Middle Low German proten (“to object, to grumble, to scold”), from Old Saxon *pratt, from Proto-West Germanic *prattu, probably ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *prattuz (“boastful talk”).
From Middle Low German prove, from Old French prueve or Medieval Latin proba. Compare English proof and German Probe.
From Middle Low German proven, from Old French prover or Medieval Latin probāre. Compare English prove and German prüfen.

parole.significato: a hump (on an animal, person etc.)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German puckel.

Via Middle Low German punct, punt from Latin pūnctum (“point”), the neuter of the participle of pungere (“to puncture”). The Low German word was also borrowed to late Old Norse punktr and Swedish punkt. Doublet of point, pointe, and punktum, and cognate with punktere (from Latin punctuo).
Likely from Middle Low German pûsten. Related to Old Norse pústr and Middle Low German puster.
From Middle Low German pensen (“think; consider”) or Middle Low German pinsen (“think; consider”), ultimately from Vulgar Latin pensāre (“consider; weigh”) via French penser (“think; consider”).

parole.significato: to concern, to be of (someone's) business
parole.testo: From Middle Low German rāken (“to hit, reach”), from Proto-West Germanic *rakōn. Probably related to the previous verb.

parole.significato: to rattle; to produce unclear, inarticulate sounds, e.g. due to mucus or fluid in the respiratory tract and often in co…
parole.testo: Probably from Middle Low German rallen. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk ralla, German rallen, Dutch rallen.
From Middle Low German ram (“target”)
From Middle Low German rame, from Old Saxon hrama. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål ramme, German Rahmen.
From Middle Low German rāmen (senses 1,2), sense 3 from the noun.

From rams + løg (“leek, onion”), borrowed from Middle Low German ramese (“ramson”), from Old Saxon *hramuso, from Proto-West Germanic *hramusō. Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk ramslauk and Swedish ramslök. Cognates amoung non-Scandinavian languages are Lithuanian kermùšė (and šermukšnis), Russian чер
From Middle Low German rar (“rare, valuable”), ultimately borrowed from Latin rārus (“loose, sparse, rare”).

parole.significato: a rest, pause, break (during a hike, travel etc.)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German rast. Second definition is from Old Norse rǫst, from Proto-Germanic *rastō, *rastijō (“rest”), from Proto-Indo-European *ros-, *res-, *erH- (“rest”).
rast + -e, from Middle Low German rasten. Compare Swedish rasta.
From Middle Low German rat (“wheel”), from Old Saxon rath.
From Middle Low German redden, from Proto-Germanic *hradjaną. Cognate with German retten.
From Middle Low German rēde, Middle Low German: gerēde, from Old Saxon *girēdi, from Proto-Germanic *raidijaz, *garaidijaz, cognate with English ready, Norwegian grei, Icelandic reiður, Swedish redo.
A mix of Middle Danish redheligh and Middle Low German redelik (“honest, suiting”).
From Middle Low German redeschap. Equivalent to red + -skab.

From Middle Low German rekenen, from Proto-Germanic *rekanōną. Cognate with English reckon, German rechnen, and Dutch rekenen. Icelandic reikna, Norwegian Nynorsk rekna, and Swedish räkna are also borrowed from Low German.

parole.significato: account, accounts (of a company or an association)
parole.testo: From regne (“to calculate”) + -skab, after Middle Low German rekenscop, German Rechenschaft.
From Middle Low German reise, from Old Saxon *reisa, from Proto-West Germanic *raisu.
From Middle Low German renne, from Proto-Germanic *rinnǭ, cognate with German Rinne (“groove”), Gothic 𐍂𐌹𐌽𐌽𐍉 (rinnō, “brook”). Derived from the verb *rinnaną (“to run”).

parole.significato: interest (money paid by borrower to lender)
parole.testo: Via Middle Low German rente (“interest”) and Old French rente (“income”) from Latin reddita, past participle of reddō (“to give back”). Cognate with English rent.
From Middle Low German riōl(e), related to German Regal. Of unknown origin, maybe ultimately from Latin rēgula (“rule, bar”).
From Middle Low German rechtverdig.
From ret + -ig + -hed, from Old Danish rættighhet, from Middle Low German rechticheit.

parole.significato: baste, tack (to sew with wide stitches to temporarily fasten pieces of cloth)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German rigen (“to put in folds”), from or related to Old Saxon rekkian (“to extend”). Distantly related to Old Norse rekja (“to unfold, unwind”), hence a doublet of række (“to reach”).
From Middle Low German ribbe, rebbe (“rib, strip”), from Proto-Germanic *ribją, cognate with German Rippe, English rib, Old Norse rif (“reef”). Doublet of rev (“reef”).

From Middle Low German ribben (“to tear”), from Proto-Germanic *rippōną, *ribōną (“to tear off”), cognate with Dutch rippen, Faroese ripa, Norwegian ripe. An intensive of Proto-Germanic *rīfaną (“to tear”).

From Middle Low German ridder (“rider, knight”), from Middle Dutch riddere, a Flemish variant of rîdere, from rîden (“to ride”) + -er. It was used to translate Old French chevalier (“knight”). The Dutch word was also borrowed to German Ritter, Old Norse riddari, and Swedish riddare.
Inherited from Old Danish ridderelik, from Middle Low German ridderlik. Equivalent to ridder + -lig.
From Middle Low German richtich, cognate with German richtig. Derived from recht (“right”).

From Middle Low German swēven, from Old Saxon *swivian, from Proto-Germanic *swibāną.
From Middle Low German sulte, from Old Saxon *sultia, from Proto-Germanic *sultijō (“salt water, brine”). Compare German Sülze and Dutch zult. Cognate with salt (“salt”).

parole.significato: to pickle, to preserve in a pickling solution
parole.testo: From Middle Low German sulten, cf. German sülzen, sulzen. Derived from the noun.
From Middle Low German sunderlik.
From Middle Low German sōdān, a compound of 1. sō (“so”) (from Old Saxon sō (“so, such that”)), and 2. dān (“done”), past participle of dōn (“to do”).
From Middle Low German sēpe, from Old Saxon sēpa, from Proto-West Germanic *saipā, from Proto-Germanic *saipǭ.
From Middle Low German seltsam. Related to native sjælden.
From Middle Low German tacke, from Old Saxon *takko, from Proto-West Germanic *takkō (“twig, branch, shoot”).
From Middle Low German talch, from Old Saxon *talg, from Proto-West Germanic *talg, from Proto-Germanic *talgaz.
From Middle Low German tallorken (“little plate”); equivalent to modern German Tellerchen.

From Old Danish tanckæ, from Middle Low German danke, from Old Saxon thanc, from Proto-Germanic *þankaz (with the initial consonant of the related verb Danish tænke (“think”)). The Middle Low German word has also been borrowed to Swedish tanke, Norwegian tanke, and Icelandic þanki.
From Middle Low German dapper, tapper. Further origin disputed. Possibly cognate with Old Norse dapr (“heavy”), German tapfer (“dauntless”) and English dapper.
From Middle Low German taske (“pocket, purse”).

parole.significato: blackboard, whiteboard, writing board (a large vertical surface to be written on with an erasable material and to be se…
parole.testo: Via Middle Low German tavele, tafele from Latin tabula (“tablet, board”).

From Middle Low German telt, from Proto-Germanic *teldą. Cognate with German Zelt and Old Norse tjald (“tent”) (whence Norwegian Bokmål tjeld, Swedish tjäll, and Danish tjæld). English tilt and Swedish tält were also borrowed from Low German.
From Middle Low German temmelik.
From to + an old dative (or genitive plural) of hob (“heap”), Calque of Middle Low German tō hōpe (“together”). Compare also Swedish ihop (“together”) and German zuhauf (“in large numbers”).
til + berede. Likely from Middle Low German tobereden. Compare Old Dutch toebereiden, German zubereiten.
Equivalent to til (“to”) + fred (“peace”). Calque of Middle Low German tōvrede, cf. German zufrieden.
By surface analysis, tilfælde + -ig. After Middle Low German tovallich.
Equivalent to til- + lade. Perhaps a calque of Middle Low German tolaten. Compare German zulassen
til + stå. After Middle Low German tostan.
Borrowed from Middle Low German toge, toch, from Old Saxon *tugi, from Proto-Germanic *tugiz. Cognate with Dutch teug, German Zug, Old English tyge. The sense "train" is derived from German Zug.
From torn + irisk (“from Middle Low German irske”).
From Middle Low German trechtäre, trechter, from Old Saxon trahtari, from Proto-West Germanic *trahtārī, from Late Latin tractārius, from Latin trāiectōrium.
From Middle Low German trampen.
Borrowed from Middle Low German trappe, from Old Saxon *trappa, from Proto-West Germanic *trappā.
From Middle Low German draven, traven.
From Middle Low German or Middle Dutch tromme, of imitative origin.
From Middle Low German trosse.

From Middle Low German trecken, which is a merger of two related verbs: Old Saxon *trekkan and *trekkian, from Proto-West Germanic *trekan (“to push, drag”) and *trakkjan (“to drag”), cognate with Dutch trekken (hence English trek). Doublet of trekke.
From Middle Low German troye, troie, possibly from Old French troie (“coat from Troyes”).

From Middle Low German tucht, from Proto-Germanic *tuhtiz (“pulling”). Cognate with German Zucht (“discipline”) and Dutch tocht (“expedition”) (whence Danish togt). Late Old Norse tykt and Swedish tukt are also borrowed from Low German. The Germanic noun is derived from the verb *teuhaną (“to lead,
From Middle Low German turtelduve.
From Old Danish thwang, from Middle Low German dwank, from Proto-Germanic *þwanguz, *þwangiz, cognate with Swedish tvång n, English thong, German Zwang, Old Norse þvengr (“thong”). Doublet of tvinge.
From Old Danish twedracht, borrowed from Middle Low German twedracht, a compound of twe- (“two”) + dracht (“pulling”). Compare Swedish tvedräkt, German Zwietracht, and Dutch tweedracht.
From Middle Low German twist.

parole.significato: (used with om) to quarrel, argue, contend, debate
parole.testo: From Middle Low German twisten. Compare Dutch twisten and Swedish tvista.
From Middle Low German twīvel.
From Middle Low German dūverīe.

From Middle Low German tuffel, shortened from pantuffel, from Medieval Latin pantofla, the first element probably from Vulgar Latin *patta (“paw, foot”). See also Italian pantofola (“slipper, shoe”), French pantoufle.

From Middle Low German tüg (“tool, clothes”), from Old Saxon *tiug, from Proto-West Germanic *teug, from Proto-Germanic *teugą, *teugą, *tiugiją (“stuff, gear, device for pulling”). Cognates include English toy and German Zeug (“stuff, gear, fabric”).
From tørst (“thirst”) + -ig, after Middle Low German dorstig.

parole.significato: to hesitate (to stop or pause respecting decision or action)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German tȫven, from Proto-Germanic *tōbijaną, cognate with Dutch toeven (“to linger”). Derived from the noun *tōbą (“hesitation”) (Icelandic tóf) and related to the verb *tabijaną (“to delay”) (Old Norse tefja).
After Middle Low German ungeachtet, from un- + geachtet (“respected”), a past participle of achten (“to respect”), which has also been borrowed to Danish (agte).
From Old Danish utlænnig (“foreign”), from Middle Low German ūtlendich, derived from ūt- (“out”) + land (“land”) + -ig, cf. German ausländisch, Ausländer and Danish udlænding with different suffixes.
After Middle Low German utstoten.
ud + sætte, from Old Danish utsættæ, perhaps from Middle Low German utsetten.
From Middle Low German ūtwerdes (“exterior, external”). Compare German auswärts. The noun is derived from the adjective.
From u- + forligne + -lig. The stem is Derived from Middle Low German vorlikenen.
u- + forskammet. Calque of Middle Low German unvorschemet.

parole.significato: undaunted; proceeding in spite of difficulty
parole.testo: Calque of Middle Low German unvordroten.
From Middle Low German unhure, ungehure. Compare German Ungeheuer, = un- + geheuer (“pleasant”). The adjective has a cognate in Old Norse hýrr (“pleasant, friendly”), from Proto-Germanic *hiurijaz.
From Middle Low German unkrūt, a compound of un- (“un-”) + krūt (“vegetables”), compare German Unkraut. The second part of the word is also borrowed to Danish krudt (“gunpowder”).
u- + lempe, from Middle Low German un(ge)limpe. Compare Swedish olämpa.
u- (“un-”) + lyst (“desire, lust”). From Middle Low German unlust, from Proto-Germanic *unlustuz (“listlessness”).

parole.significato: the act of making an effort
parole.testo: From Middle Low German ungemak.

parole.significato: Inseparable verb prefix indicating removing something from the object, from, away from, off.
parole.testo: Partly a loan from Middle Low German ent-, unt-, from Proto-Germanic *andi- (cf. German ent-), and partly an abbreviation of Old Norse undan, from Proto-Germanic *undanē (“down under”).
From Middle Low German underdanich.
From Middle Low German underkopen.
From Middle Low German unterlegen. Compare German unterliegen.
From under- + rette, after Middle Low German underrichten.

parole.significato: at the bottom, bottom-most, lowest (all senses)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German unterst.
From under- + trykke, from Middle Low German underdrucken. Compare Latin supprimere.

parole.significato: to teach, to instruct, to educate
parole.testo: From Middle Low German underwisen. Compare Dutch onderwijzen.

parole.significato: to conceive (a child or an idea)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German untvangen, entvangen. Cf. German empfangen (“to receive, conceive”). The second part of this word is from Proto-Germanic *fanhaną (“to take, catch”).
After Middle Low German entvlen. Compare Dutch ontvlieden.
Equivalent to und- (“away”) + gå (“to go”), from Old Danish untgaa. Calque of Middle Low German entgān, compare German entgehen.
und- + lade; from older underlade, from Middle Low German underlaten. Compare Norwegian unnlate, Swedish underlåta.

parole.significato: to be reluctant; refrain from doing something (due to modesty, tact etc.)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German sik untsen (“to look away”).
After Middle Low German untseggen, entseggen.
From undskylde (“to excuse”), Middle Low German entschulden. Cognate with Norwegian unnskyld and German entschuldigen.
From Middle Low German entschulden.
After Middle Low German entsetten. Compare German entsetzen, Dutch ontzetten.

und- (“away”) + være (“to be”). A remodelling of Middle Low German entberen, Middle Low German untberen, cf. German entbehren. The second part of this word is Proto-Germanic *beraną (“to carry, bear”). Swedish umbära was also borrowed from Low German.

From Middle Low German ūr (“watch, clock”), which was borrowed, via Middle Dutch ūre, from Old French houre (“hour”), from Latin hōra (“hour”) and ultimately Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “season, hour”). The German Uhr (“watch”) was also borrowed from Low German.

parole.significato: sexual immorality, fornication (a lack of discipline)
parole.testo: Equivalent to u- + tugt. From Middle Low German untucht. Compare Dutch ontucht.
From Middle Low German wacht, wachte, from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō, cognate with German Wacht. Norwegian vakt and Swedish vakt are also borrowed from Low German.
From Middle Low German wachtele.
From Middle Low German wal or Dutch wal (“coast, shore”), from Latin vallum. Doublet of vold.
From Middle Low German wanderen. Compare English wander.
Equivalent to van- (“badly”) + vittig (“minded”) or rather vanvid (“insanity”) + -ig. After Middle Low German wanwittich, cf. also German wahnwitzig.

parole.significato: to last, take (to have a certain duration)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German wāren, from Proto-West Germanic *waʀōn, *weʀēn (“to stay, remain”), cognate with German währen. Derived from the verb *wesaną (“to be”) (Danish være).
Perhaps from Middle Low German warich.
From Middle Low German warwulf, from Old Saxon werwulf.
From Middle Low German watersucht, a calque of Latin hydrōps, from Ancient Greek ὕδρωψ (húdrōps).
From veder- (“re-”) + kvæge (“to quicken”), calque of Middle Low German wedderquicken. Compare also Swedish vederkvicka.
From Middle Low German wolberāden, German wohlberaten. From wohl + beraten.
From Middle Low German wolstant.
From Middle Low German wēmōt, whence also German Wehmut (which see). Analysable as ve (“woe”) + mod (“mood”).
vemod + -ig, after Middle Low German wemodich.

parole.significato: science, scholarly knowledge, scholarship (collective discipline of learning acquired through any scholarly method; tot…
parole.testo: From Middle Low German wetenschop. Equivalent to viden + -skab. Compare Norwegian Bokmål vitenskap, Swedish vetenskap, German Wissenschaft, Dutch wetenschap.
From Middle Low German wichtich, from wichte.
From Middle Low German willekor.
From Middle Low German wenken, winken.
From Middle Low German wirok. Compare German Weihrauch (“frankincense”).
From Middle Low German witlik, mixed with Old Norse vitrligr (“wise”).

From Middle Low German wittich (“sensible, intelligent”), derived from the noun witte, wit, from Proto-Germanic *witją. Compare German witzig from Witz. The current sense from French spirituel (“witty”) via German witzig (“funny, humo(u)rous”).
From Middle Low German wachten, derived from the noun wacht, wachte (“guard”), from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō.
From vogte (“to guard”) + -er, or borrowed from Middle Low German wachter, derived from the noun wacht, wachte (“guard”), from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō. Compare German Wächter.
From Middle Low German wal, from Proto-Germanic *wallaz, *wallą, an early borrowing of Latin vallum; cognate with English wall, German Wall.

From Middle Danish waaghe, wogæ, wowæ, from Middle Low German wagen, from Proto-Germanic *wagōną. Cognate with German wagen, Dutch wagen, Old Norse vaga (“to waddle”) (late Old Norse voga and Swedish våga are also borrowed from Low German). Doublet of vugge.
From Middle Low German wāch m, wāge f, from Proto-Germanic *wēgaz, cognate with English waw (obsolete), Dutch waag f, Old Norse vágr (“sea; bay”). Doublet of våg.
From Middle Low German wrak, probably from Old Saxon *wrak, derived from wrekan. Compare English wrack, German Wrack and Swedish vrak.
From Middle Low German wraken or German bracken (“to reject”), ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *wrekan (“to drive out”).
From Middle Low German wāninge.

parole.significato: a competition where the goal is to drive, ride, cycle or run the fastest
parole.testo: From Middle Low German weddelop. Equivalent to vædde + løb.
From Middle Low German wēke.
From Middle Low German wēgeren, weigeren, from Proto-West Germanic *waigrōn (“to be stubborn”).

From Old Danish wict, wæct, from Middle Low German wicht, from Proto-Germanic *wihtiz. The old Nordic form of the word is found in Old Danish wæt. Cognate with English weight, Latin vectis. Swedish vikt is also borrowed from Low German.
From Middle Low German wechter, wachter, derived from wacht (“watch”), from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō. Compare German Wächter. Norwegian vekter and Swedish väktare are also borrowed from Low German.
From Middle Low German wechtich. Equivalent to vægt + -ig.
From Middle Low German wech, derived from Middle Low German weg (“way”), from Old Saxon weg. Compare Old Norse á veg, English away and German weg.
From Middle Low German weldich, whence also Swedish väldig, Norwegian veldig. Maybe influenced by vælde.
From Middle Low German werdīe. Cognates include Swedish värde, Norwegian Bokmål verdi. Related to værd
From Middle Low German werk or Middle Dutch werk, cognate with Old High German werah, werc, German Werg. Originally the same word as the first one.
From Middle Low German wert (“host”), from Proto-Germanic *werduz, cognate with German Wirt, Dutch waard, Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌳𐌿𐍃 (wairdus). Swedish värd is also borrowed from Low German.
From Middle Low German wesen (“existence”), German Wesen (“essence, character”), originally an infinitive, from Proto-Germanic *wesaną (“to be”) (= Danish være).
From Middle Low German wesentlich, wesentlich. By surface analysis, væsen + -lig.

Borrowed from Middle Low German ūteren (“challenge, declare, drive out, give away”), compare German äußern and English utter. Derived from Middle Low German ūtere (“outer”), Old High German ūzaro, Old English ūtera, an adjective formed to the adverb Proto-Germanic *ūt (“out”).
From Middle Low German openbār, cf. German offenbar, from open + -bar, offen (“open”) + -bar.
From Middle Low German openbāren, cf. German offenbaren, from openbar + -en, offenbar + -en.

From Middle Low German orsake (“reason, cause”), related to German Ursache. It is a compound of or- + sake / ur- + Sache, from Proto-Germanic *uz- (“out”) and *sakō (“case”). From Middle Low German echt, whence also German echt (“lawful”). Originally a compound of 1. Middle Low German ē (“law, marriage”) (German Ehe (“marriage”)), from Proto-Germanic *aiwǭ, *aiwaz (“law”), and 2. German -haft, from Proto-Germanic *haftaz (“captured, afflicted”). The verb is derived from
From Middle Low German echtschap (“marriage”). Compare Norwegian Bokmål ekteskap, Swedish äktenskap. Equivalent to ægte + -skab.
From Middle Low German engesten.
By surface analysis, ære + -bar. From Middle Low German erbar (“noble”).
ære (“honour”) + -lig. From Middle Low German erlich. Compare German ehrlich.
Borrowed from Middle Low German esel, from Old Saxon esil, from Proto-West Germanic *asil, from Latin asellus. Largely replaced the inherited Old Norse asni.

parole.significato: to urge (to press the mind or will of)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German êschen, eischen, from Old Saxon ēskōn.

From Middle Low German ôgenblik. Compare Norwegian Bokmål øyeblikk, Dutch ogenblik, German Augenblick, Icelandic augnablik, Swedish ögonblick, Yiddish אויגנבליק (oygnblik), and English eyeblink. Equivalent to øje (“eye”) + blik (“look”).

parole.significato: to practise (with or without an object)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German ȫven, from Old Saxon ōvian, from Proto-Germanic *ōbijaną (“to do, practise”). Cognate with German üben.
